description_full: Embraer S.A., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the design, development, manufacture, and sale of aircraft and systems worldwide. The company operates through Commercial Aviation; Defense & Security; Executive Aviation; Services & Support; and Other segments. The Commercial Aviation segment develops, produces, and sells commercial jets. The Defense & Security segment develops and produces military aircraft; and is involved in research and development of software and integrated information systems, communications, border monitoring and surveillance, space systems/satellites, and aircraft modernization services and services support, as well as command, control, communications, computer, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance systems. The Executive Aviation segment develops, produces, and sells executive jets. The Service & Support segment provides field and technical support, flight operations solutions, aircraft modification, materials management, maintenance solutions, and training programs. The Other segment engages in the supply of structural parts and hydraulic systems; production of agricultural crop-spraying aircraft; development and certification of eVTOLs; creation of a maintenance and service network, and air traffic control system for eVTOLs; development and manufacture of electrical propulsion systems; cybersecurity; and software and technical products. Additionally, the company is involved in leasing of used aircraft; pilot, mechanic, and crew training; engineering services; retail trade, maintenance, and repair of computer products; information technology consulting, data processing, application service providers, and internet hosting; and fabrication of aircraft interiors. The company was formerly known as Embraer-Empresa Brasileira de Aeronáutica S.A. and changed its name to Embraer S.A. in November 2010. Embraer S.A. was founded in 1969 and is headquartered in São Paulo, Brazil.

financial_summary: Embraer S.A. is a large-cap industrials business with a $13.4B market cap on $7.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +19% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 32% against a 11% cost of capital — a 21-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 17% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $683M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.42× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.3%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 16% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 75% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 1.33, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 3.59 vs 5y 1.60), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $100.5M traded a day, and interest is running hot at 2.0x its yearly average volume.

val: The stock trades 35% below its DCF fair value of $29.10, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 40%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $13.95 to $68.30 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Industrials peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 2.9 vs 13.3, richer on P/E 33.7 vs 23.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 62% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $24.55 on average, 30% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 32% clears the cost of capital of 11.0% by 21pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.12).
It runs a 17% gross margin and converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.42x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.8x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 18.6% over 3 years and 15.0% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 26%).
At current returns, reinvesting 36% of profits supports about 11.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
It has missed earnings estimates by 42.0% on average.
Analysts expect 42.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 47%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.3% (1.3% in dividends).
people: With about 21,122 employees, each generates about $359K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 3.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $32K of free cash flow per employee.
